prompt: Why may a public good not be provided by a free market?

options.label: A
options.text: The costs of supplying public goods are necessarily too high.

options.label: B
options.text: Each beneficiary must receive exactly the same value from provision.

options.label: C
options.text: Private suppliers cannot physically produce goods used by many people.

options.label: D
options.text: Beneficiaries can avoid payment, leaving suppliers without sufficient revenue.

explanation: A public good is non-excludable, so people may wait for others to pay while still expecting to benefit. This free-rider problem can prevent a private supplier from collecting sufficient revenue, causing non-provision.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may a merit good be under-consumed in a free market?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers cannot legally buy the good from a private supplier.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers may underestimate the benefits they receive from consumption.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers may overestimate the benefits they receive from consumption.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumers cannot buy additional units because supply is fixed.

explanation: The syllabus links merit goods to imperfect information. If consumers do not appreciate the full benefits to themselves, the quantity they choose may be below the quantity they would choose if fully informed.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why may a demerit good be over-consumed?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers can obtain the product without paying the supplier.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers receive no personal benefit from the product, so even fully informed consumers would never choose to purchase it.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers are prevented from buying the product privately.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumers may underestimate the personal harm caused by consumption.

explanation: Demerit-good over-consumption arises when imperfect information causes consumers to underestimate the disadvantages of consumption. Their chosen quantity can therefore exceed the fully informed quantity.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government is concerned that low-income households cannot afford an essential medicine at the market price. What is the clearest reason for controlling its price?

options.text: To improve affordability for consumers.

options.label: B
options.text: To improve income security for producers.

options.label: C
options.text: To correct underestimated health risks.

options.label: D
options.text: To finance a non-excludable service.

explanation: A government may control the price of an essential good for equity reasons, especially when the market price makes access difficult for low-income consumers.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government wants to prevent farm incomes falling sharply when the market price of a crop is very low. What is the clearest reason for controlling the crop price?

options.text: To support the incomes of crop producers.

options.text: To lower food costs for crop consumers.

options.label: C
options.text: To correct underestimated health benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: To fund services through compulsory payments.

explanation: A minimum or supported price can be motivated by a desire to protect producer incomes when the market price is regarded as too low. The question concerns the reason for intervention, not the later effects of the control.

prompt: Which characteristic of a public good most directly creates the free-rider problem?

options.text: Imperfect consumer information

options.label: B
options.text: A high market price

options.label: C
options.text: Non-excludability

options.label: D
options.text: Rivalry in consumption

explanation: Non-excludability means a non-payer cannot easily be prevented from enjoying the benefit once the good is provided. This weakens the incentive to pay voluntarily.

prompt: A coastal warning siren can be heard by all nearby residents whether or not they pay. Why might government intervention be required?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Non-payers benefit, limiting the revenue a supplier can collect.

options.label: D
options.text: Residents underestimate the personal harm from hearing warnings.

explanation: The inability to exclude non-payers makes voluntary market financing difficult. Even if many residents value the warning system, each has an incentive to rely on others to pay.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Parents underestimate the future earnings benefits of an optional training course for their children. What government concern does this most directly create?

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Over-consumption of a demerit good

options.label: D

prompt: Consumers underestimate the long-term health costs of a highly processed snack and therefore buy more of it than they would if fully informed. What is the reason for possible government intervention?

options.text: Over-consumption of a demerit good

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Under-consumption of a public good

options.label: D
options.text: Non-provision caused by non-rivalry alone

prompt: Why might a government control the price of a basic household good even when a market price exists?

options.label: A
options.text: Equilibrium prices establish that a good is non-excludable.

options.label: B
options.text: Price controls remove the need to ration scarce goods.

options.label: C
options.text: Market prices may conflict with an affordability objective.

options.label: D
options.text: Controlled prices make consumption non-rival for all users.

explanation: Price controls may be introduced for distributional or equity reasons. A market can clear and yet the government may judge the resulting price to be too high for some consumers or too low for some producers.

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: Street lighting can have public-good characteristics. When households expect to benefit without paying, voluntary payment may be insufficient and the good may not be provided privately.

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: Correcting over-consumption caused by imperfect information

options.text: The service may remain unprovided despite being valued.

prompt: What is the information problem behind government concern about merit and demerit goods?

options.label: C

options.label: D

explanation: A rise in informed consumption is consistent with a merit-good information problem: consumers originally undervalued the benefit and chose too little.

prompt: A service changes from non-excludable to excludable after a new access-control technology is introduced, while remaining non-rival. Which effect on the reason for government intervention is most likely?

options.label: A
options.text: The provider can now charge users, weakening the non-provision rationale.

options.label: B
options.text: The provider can now produce without sacrificing other resource uses.

options.label: C
options.text: The service now causes consumers to underestimate its personal harms.

options.label: D
options.text: The service now becomes harder to finance through user payments.

explanation: The central financing problem is inability to exclude non-payers. Once exclusion becomes practical, voluntary private provision is more feasible even if the service remains non-rival.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government wants people to consume more of a service even after they have been given complete information and still choose not to do so. Which judgement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The service necessarily becomes non-rival because consumers reject it.

options.label: B
options.text: The service necessarily becomes non-excludable because consumers reject it.

options.label: C
options.text: The case depends on a preferred outcome beyond correcting misinformation.

options.label: D
options.text: Complete information must make consumers choose precisely the quantity preferred by government, regardless of their individual valuations.

explanation: The syllabus links merit-good under-consumption to imperfect information. If consumers remain fully informed and still choose less than the government prefers, the remaining argument is more paternalistic or normative than informational.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A high-sugar product is heavily consumed. Consumers correctly understand all personal health risks and can explain them accurately. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: Full knowledge of personal health risks establishes that extra consumption by one buyer cannot reduce the benefit available to any other buyer.

options.label: B
options.text: Knowledge of personal risks establishes that consumption is non-excludable.

options.label: C
options.text: High consumption alone does not demonstrate an imperfect-information problem.

options.label: D
options.text: High consumption alone establishes that personal benefits are underestimated.

explanation: The AS syllabus identifies over-consumption arising from imperfect information. If consumers are fully informed, high consumption by itself does not demonstrate that specific market-failure mechanism.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: The diagram shows an essential utility with equilibrium price Pe and a lower line P* labelled “maximum socially acceptable price”. Which statement best explains the intervention rationale?

options.label: A
options.text: The equilibrium price alone establishes that consumers underestimate personal benefits, even when no information about their knowledge is supplied.

options.label: B
options.text: The equilibrium price establishes that consumption is non-excludable.

options.label: C
options.text: The government judges the equilibrium price inconsistent with its objective.

options.label: D
options.text: The government’s preferred price eliminates the product’s resource scarcity.

explanation: The phrase “socially acceptable” signals a value judgement. A government may control prices because it prioritises affordability or equity rather than because equilibrium has failed to occur.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which pairing of price-control objective and group protected is most logically consistent?

options.label: A
options.text: Maximum price — producer income; minimum price — consumer affordability.

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum price — non-excludability; minimum price — underestimated benefits.

options.label: C
options.text: Maximum price — underestimated harms; minimum price — free riding.

options.label: D
options.text: Maximum price — consumer affordability; minimum price — producer income.

explanation: A ceiling is associated with limiting what consumers pay, while a floor is associated with preventing the price received by sellers or workers from falling below a chosen level.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Why can tax-financed government provision solve a public-good funding problem without making the good a “free good”?

options.label: A
options.text: Taxation removes the opportunity cost of producing public goods.

options.label: B
options.text: Compulsory finance limits free riding while production still uses resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Taxation ensures every beneficiary receives an equal share of value.

options.label: D
options.text: Compulsory finance makes each additional consumer reduce others’ available benefits.

explanation: Government finance changes the payment mechanism, not the scarcity of resources. The good still has an opportunity cost, but compulsory finance prevents non-payers from undermining provision.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A road is initially uncongested and open to everyone. Later it becomes congested and electronic tolling makes exclusion easy. What is the most defensible conclusion about intervention for public-good non-provision?

options.label: A
options.text: Exclusion permits charging users, weakening the pure-public-good funding argument.

options.label: B
options.text: Congestion increases non-rivalry, strengthening the pure-public-good funding argument.

options.label: C
options.text: Tolling removes scarcity, eliminating the opportunity cost of road provision.

options.label: D
options.text: Congestion prevents exclusion, eliminating opportunities to collect user payments.

explanation: Congestion introduces rivalry, and tolling introduces excludability. Both changes move the road away from the pure-public-good case that most strongly supports the non-provision argument.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A student chooses one year of training because she thinks the benefit lasts one year. Reliable information shows the benefit lasts ten years, and she then chooses three years. What is the relevant government-intervention reason?

options.label: A
options.text: The original choice exceeded the fully informed quantity because the student underestimated personal harms, explaining the later increase in training.

options.label: B
options.text: Initial consumption fell below informed consumption because benefits were underestimated.

options.label: C
options.text: Information reduced the resource costs of supplying every training course.

options.label: D
options.text: Information made training non-excludable and caused suppliers to stop production.

explanation: This is a direct merit-good information problem. The consumer underestimated the duration of the personal benefit and therefore initially chose too little.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO2 Analysis

options.text: Activity R

options.label: B
options.text: Activity P

options.label: C
options.text: Activity Q

options.label: D

prompt: A government is choosing between controlling the price of a staple food and doing nothing. Which evidence most directly supports the reason for intervention based on consumer affordability?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers fully understand the food’s nutritional benefits.

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers can be excluded unless they pay.

options.label: C
options.text: Low-income households cannot afford the market price.

options.label: D
options.text: Producers can accurately calculate their production costs.

explanation: The 3.1.3 rationale concerns the level of the market price relative to a policy objective such as affordability. The other facts do not themselves justify price control.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A privately produced flood-warning app becomes available only to paying subscribers, while a separate public siren remains audible to everyone. Which service has the stronger non-provision rationale?

options.label: A
options.text: The siren, because beneficiaries can obtain warnings without paying.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither, because warning services have no opportunity cost of production.

options.label: C
options.text: The app, because subscribers can be charged for receiving warnings.

options.label: D
options.text: Both equally, because technological services necessarily have non-excludable benefits.

explanation: The siren has the stronger free-rider problem because access cannot be restricted. The app can link payment to access, so private provision is easier.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consumers originally choose 80 units of a product. After complete risk information they choose 50 units, with all other relevant conditions unchanged. What does the 30-unit difference represent conceptually?

options.label: A
options.text: A shortage of income received by producers that must be corrected by imposing a minimum legal price above the market equilibrium.

options.label: B
options.text: Possible over-consumption resulting from underestimated personal harm.

options.label: C
options.text: A funding shortfall arising from non-excludability and free riding.

options.label: D
options.text: A resource saving establishing zero opportunity cost of production.

explanation: The fall in desired consumption after full information is evidence that the original choice exceeded the fully informed choice. That is the over-consumption mechanism in 3.1.2.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A government proposes a price floor for a farm product because “society should preserve rural incomes”. What type of reasoning is central to this justification?

options.label: A
options.text: A positive claim about the crop’s non-excludability.

options.label: B
options.text: A factual claim that consumers currently underestimate the personal benefits of eating the crop, rather than a preference about distribution.

options.label: C
options.text: A normative judgement about the acceptable income distribution.

options.label: D
options.text: A normative judgement about the crop’s non-rivalry.

explanation: The statement expresses a judgement about whose incomes should be protected. Price control can therefore be motivated by equity and social priorities, not only by technical market conditions.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO2 Analysis

prompt: The diagram shows a farm market with equilibrium price Pe below a line Pf labelled “price required to meet the government’s producer-income objective”. Which statement best describes the reason for intervention?

options.label: A
options.text: The equilibrium price falls short of the government’s income-support target.

options.label: B
options.text: The low equilibrium price makes consumption non-rival between crop consumers.

options.label: C
options.text: The low equilibrium price establishes that consumers underestimate personal benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: The equilibrium price establishes that producers cannot exclude non-paying consumers.

explanation: The labelled income objective makes the rationale distributional. The free-market price is below the level the government considers consistent with its producer-income goal.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement best explains why a private firm can physically produce a public good but the free market may still fail to provide it?

options.label: A
options.text: Non-rival consumption prevents the firm from physically producing the good.

options.label: B
options.text: Public goods require government-owned resources rather than privately owned resources.

options.label: C
options.text: Non-excludability removes the scarce-resource costs associated with producing the good.

options.label: D
options.text: Non-excludability can prevent the firm collecting sufficient revenue.

explanation: Non-provision is a financing and incentive problem, not a claim that private firms lack the technical ability to produce the service.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.1 addressing the non-provision of public goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A product is harmful in large quantities, but consumers are fully informed and choose the same quantity before and after receiving additional information. Which description is safest?

options.label: A
options.text: Potential harm alone establishes over-consumption caused by imperfect information.

options.label: B
options.text: Potential harm alone establishes non-excludability and a public-good funding problem.

options.label: C
options.text: These observations do not establish over-consumption caused by imperfect information.

options.label: D
options.text: Unchanged consumption establishes that consumers underestimate the product’s personal benefits.

explanation: The syllabus definition links demerit-good over-consumption to imperfect information. Harmfulness alone does not show that consumers are choosing more than they would if fully informed.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A city considers controlling taxi fares because it wants fares to remain affordable, even though the taxi market clears. Which principle is most relevant?

options.label: A
options.text: A market-clearing price necessarily satisfies every government equity objective because equality of quantities guarantees affordability for all households.

options.label: B
options.text: An affordability concern necessarily establishes consumers underestimate the service’s benefits.

options.label: C
options.text: A controlled fare necessarily makes taxi journeys a non-excludable service.

options.label: D
options.text: Equity objectives may justify intervention even though the market clears.

explanation: A market can reach equilibrium yet produce a distribution of access that government judges unacceptable. Price control can therefore reflect an equity objective.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government has evidence that a merit good is under-consumed because consumers underestimate its benefits. Which new evidence would most weaken that explanation?

options.label: A
options.text: Information leaves desired consumption unchanged.

options.label: B
options.text: Production requires resources with alternative uses.

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers pay a positive price per purchase.

options.label: D
options.text: Private businesses supply the service to consumers.

explanation: If fully informed consumers do not want more, the claim that missing benefit information caused under-consumption is weakened. Private supply and scarcity do not by themselves contradict the merit-good rationale.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: A government observes a high market price. Which additional fact is most important before concluding that price control is justified based on consumer affordability?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether scarce resources are used in production.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether demand decreases when the market price rises.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether suppliers receive revenue when selling the product, regardless of any government objective about affordability for low-income consumers.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether the price conflicts with a defined policy objective.

explanation: A high price alone is not a complete reason for intervention. The government needs a policy objective that the price is preventing, such as access, equity or income stability.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: After consumers receive accurate information about a demerit good, their preferred consumption falls from 70 units to 45 units. Which statement is most defensible?

options.label: A
options.text: The 25-unit reduction is consistent with earlier information-related over-consumption.

options.label: B
options.text: The decrease in consumption demonstrates that private providers cannot supply the product and all production must transfer to government agencies.

options.label: C
options.text: The reduction establishes that a binding price ceiling was introduced.

options.label: D
options.text: The reduction establishes that additional consumers no longer reduce others’ benefits.

explanation: The comparison isolates the effect of better information on the consumer’s own preferred quantity. A lower informed choice is consistent with prior over-consumption arising from underestimated harm.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.2 addressing the over-consumption of demerit goods and the under-consumption of merit goods | AO3 Evaluation

prompt: Which statement best captures the limit of the argument that governments should control every unusually high market price?

options.label: A
options.text: High prices establish that production has no opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: High prices alone do not establish a policy justification.

options.label: C
options.text: High prices establish that consumers underestimate all personal benefits.

options.label: D
options.text: High prices alone establish that non-paying consumers cannot be excluded.

explanation: Price control is not justified merely because a price is high. The economic rationale must connect the market outcome to a government objective or identified problem.
reference: 3.1 Reasons for government intervention in markets | 3.1.3 controlling prices in markets | AO3 Evaluation
